Name: logit_lens_language_leak
Title: Reading the Interlingua: Do Intermediate Logits Reveal a Language-Neutral or Dominant-Language Code?
Short Hypothesis: Applying the unembedding to intermediate layers (logit lens) in non-dominant-language processing yields dominant-language tokens not because computation is dominant-language-based, but because the unembedding is dominant-language-biased; a language-fair lens (per-language calibrated unembedding) reveals the intermediate code is more language-neutral than raw logit lens suggests.
Related Work: Wendler et al. use logit lens to argue for English-centric processing. We critically test whether that conclusion is an unembedding artifact by building a language-calibrated lens, distinguishing genuine dominant-language computation from readout bias—an important methodological correction with substantive implications.
Abstract: The claim that models 'think in English' rests largely on logit-lens readouts showing dominant-language tokens in intermediate layers. We hypothesize this is partly an artifact of a dominant-language-biased unembedding, not evidence that intermediate computation is dominant-language-based. We propose a language-fair lens: calibrate the unembedding per language (e.g., whiten/normalize per-language token statistics or learn a per-language readout) and re-examine intermediate representations. We predict the fair lens shows substantially more language-neutrality (or target-language content) in the middle layers than the raw logit lens, indicating the intermediate code is more abstract than 'English tokens.' We quantify the gap between raw and fair-lens language attributions across layers and languages, and validate the fair lens against causal probes (which language's content is causally present). Metrics: raw vs fair-lens dominant-language token fraction by layer, agreement of fair lens with causal concept probes, and residual dominant-language content after calibration. This offers a methodological correction to a prominent multilingual interpretability claim and sharpens conclusions about latent-language processing.
Experiments: Reproduce raw logit-lens dominant-language token fractions across layers for non-dominant-language inputs.
Build a language-fair lens: per-language unembedding calibration (whitening / learned readout).
Compare raw vs fair-lens dominant-language attribution by layer/language.
Validate fair lens against causal concept probes (which language's content is causally present).
Quantify residual dominant-language content after calibration.
Test on models with different dominant languages.
Controls: dominant-language inputs (should read dominant either way); random calibration.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Calibration could over-correct, hiding genuine dominant-language content.
Defining a 'fair' lens is itself a modeling choice with assumptions.
Logit lens is inherently limited for nonlinear representations.
Conclusions may depend on the calibration method.
